newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkey-Cyprus missile row hots up.
newsitem.headline: Turkey-Cyprus missile row hots up.

text.p: Turkey on Friday again threatened military action against Cyprus to stop it deploying Russian missiles and said it might occupy an abandoned tourist resort on the island if the Cypriot government did not back down.
Foreign Minister Tansu Ciller said Turkey could knock out an anti-aircraft missile system the Greek Cypriot government plans to install under a deal made with Russia last weekend.
"These offensive missiles will definitely not be deployed. If they are deployed we will do what is needed, if that means they need to be hit they will be hit," Ciller told reporters.
Ciller accused Greece of encouraging the Cypriot government to create a missile crisis in the Mediterranean.
NATO allies Ankara and Athens almost came to blows a year ago in a row over a deserted islet in the Aegean Sea.
Despite the Turkish threats and U.S. and British pressure to scrap the deal with Russia, Cypriot President Glafcos Clerides gave no sign he intended to back down.
"We are not negotiating the S-300 missile system," Clerides told reporters in the divided capital Nicosia.
The Cypriot government insists the S-300 missiles are defensive and its foreign minister noted they would not be delivered for at least 16 months anyway.
Turkey summoned the Russian ambassador to the Foreign Ministry in Ankara to ask Moscow to abandon the missile deal but Moscow's envoy Vadim Kuznetsow said he saw no grounds to do so.

Turkish Cypriot leader Rauf Denktash added to the war of words in Nicosia with a statement warning of moves to integrate the abandoned "ghost resort" of Varosha into the Turkish sector of the island if the rocket plan was not scrapped.

Varosha -- once the island's top tourist resort and mostly owned by Greek Cypriots -- has been left abandoned but still under Turkish military control since 1974 when Turkey invaded northern Cyprus after a coup in Nicosia engineered by the military junta then ruling Greece.

Turkey has some 30,000 troops in the northern third of Cyprus which declared itself a Turkish Cypriot state but is only recognised by Ankara. The internationally recognised Greek Cypriot government in the south commands a national guard of over 10,000 troops and is backed militarily by Athens.

"Every day we are hearing one or two new threats. We are not going to follow the line of Turkey. We are going to concentrate on a political solution to the Cyprus problem," Cypriot Foreign Minister Alecos Michaelides told Reuters.
Nonetheless Cyprus stocks plunged 1.75 percent over the week on concern about the missile dispute.
Washington is to send an envoy to the island over the weekend to try to reduce the tension.
United Nations Secretary-General Kofi Annan expressed concern over the mounting tension on the island and called for maximum restraint.

In a statement issued through a spokesman he reminded all sides that the U.N. Charter forbade the threat or use of force and underscored the importance of "carefully prepared face-to-face talks" between the leaders of the Greek Cypriot and Turkish Cypriot communities.
